text:
A: Hi.
B: Hello.
A: Dominic. I'm in Walthamstow.
B: Agnieszka. Wakefield.
A: Rebecca said I'd get you at some point. She said you told her the sea's for fish.
B: It is for fish. February. She swims in it. I said what I think.
A: Yeah. I'm with you on that.
B: Good. What do you do?
A: I run a post-production company in Soho. Editing, colour, sound. Adverts, mostly, some TV.
B: The fox. Callum told me. Everybody is talking about this fox.
A: [laughs] It's following me round today. I've done other things, honestly.
B: But the fox is the one people remember. This is how it is. I teach maths twenty years and the kids remember that I shouted once in 2014.
A: What did you shout?
B: "Sit down." Very loud. A boy was standing on a table. Now it's a legend at the school.
A: Fair enough. That's a good legend.
B: Mm.
A: Do you like it? Teaching?
B: The teaching, yes. Explaining something, and you see the face, they understand. That is good. The rest, no. Data drops, meetings, someone from senior leadership with a PowerPoint about "learning journeys". Twice they wanted me to be head of year. Twice I said no.
A: Yeah. That's sort of me with the business side. I like the edit suite. The spreadsheets I leave to my business partner. If it was up to me we'd have gone bust in about a week.
B: At least you know. Most people in management don't know.
A: [laughs] I'll take that.
B: What do you do when you are not working? You look like you are always working.
A: That's the third time someone's said that today. Er, cinema, mostly. On my own. Small cinemas. I saw a Korean thriller last week that was, er, quite good.
B: Thriller. With a detective?
A: Sort of. There's a police officer, but he's useless, which is the point. It's more about this family in one flat, and something's wrong with the neighbour, and you spend two hours not sure who's lying. By the end you don't trust anyone in it, including the kid. It's very tight. Nothing wasted. Every shot's doing a job.
B: I like this. I read crime novels, Polish and Scandinavian. And I watch every detective series on the TV. My husband used to say I always know who did it by twenty minutes.
A: Do you?
B: Usually. In British dramas, it's the famous actor who is in the first episode for only one scene. Always him.
A: [laughs] Yeah. That's a casting problem. Once you've paid for someone, you have to use them.
B: So I am right.
A: You're right. Don't tell anyone in the industry.
B: I don't know anyone in the industry. Only you.
A: Then it's safe.
B: You go to galleries also? You have this print behind you, the orange.
A: Yeah, a bit. Openings, studios in East London. I haven't hung that one yet.
B: In Wakefield we have the Hepworth. I went once when it opened. A lot of concrete.
A: It is a lot of concrete. I've been, actually. The building's alright. Some of the Hepworth pieces are, er, very good.
B: Maybe. I looked at the concrete, I looked at the river, I went home.
A: That's a review, to be fair.
B: Short reviews are best. Like my marking. "Show working." Done.
A: What's the Polish crime writer I should read? If I was going to start somewhere.
B: Somewhere easy, translated. There is one, Miłoszewski, the prosecutor Szacki books. He is miserable, everybody is miserable, it rains. You would like it.
A: Why would I—
B: Because you look like you would like miserable people in the rain. I mean it nicely.
